title: Unit of account, executory contracts and the substance of contracts
summary: How rights and obligations are grouped for accounting, how executory contracts are treated, and why substance matters in contracts.

chunks.heading: Unit of account
chunks.explanation_md:
The **unit of account** is the right or group of rights, the obligation or group of obligations, or the group of rights and obligations, **to which recognition criteria and measurement concepts are applied**.

A unit is chosen when deciding how recognition and measurement will apply to an asset or liability and its income and expenses. It can differ for recognition and measurement: contracts may be **recognised individually but measured as a portfolio**. For presentation and disclosure items may be **aggregated or separated**. If part of an asset or liability is transferred, the unit may change so that the transferred and retained components become separate units.

The unit is chosen to give **useful information**:

(a) **Relevant.** Treating a group as a single unit may be more relevant if the rights and obligations **cannot or are unlikely to be sold separately**, **do not expire in different patterns**, have **similar economic characteristics and risks**, or are **used together** to produce cash flows and measured by their interdependent cash flows.
(b) **Faithful** to the **substance** of the transaction. Rights from different sources may need to be treated as one unit, or those from a single source separated.

Cost also constrains the choice: costs **rise as the unit gets smaller**, so rights or obligations from the same source are separated only if the information is more useful and the benefits outweigh the costs.

key_terms.meaning: The right or group of rights, the obligation or group of obligations, or group of rights and obligations to which recognition criteria and measurement concepts are applied.

chunks.heading: Executory contracts
chunks.explanation_md:
An **executory contract** is a contract, or part of one, that is **equally unperformed**: **neither party has fulfilled any obligations**, or both have partly fulfilled them **to an equal extent**.

It creates a **combined right and obligation to exchange economic resources**. They are interdependent and cannot be separated, so together they form **a single asset or liability**:

- an **asset** if the terms of the exchange are currently **favourable**;
- a **liability** if the terms are currently **unfavourable**.

Whether it appears in the statements depends on the **recognition criteria** (Chapter 5) and the **measurement basis** (Chapter 6), including any test for whether the contract is **onerous**.

**When performance starts.** To the extent either party performs, the contract is **no longer executory**. If the entity **performs first**, that changes its combined right and obligation into a **right to receive** a resource: an **asset**. If the other party **performs first**, it changes into an **obligation to transfer** a resource: a **liability**.

key_terms.meaning: A contract, or part of one, that is equally unperformed: neither party has performed, or both have partly performed to an equal extent.

chunks.exam_line: An executory contract is a single asset (favourable terms) or liability (unfavourable terms). If the entity performs first it has a right to receive, an asset; if the other party performs first it has an obligation, a liability.

chunks.heading: Substance of contractual rights and obligations
chunks.explanation_md:
The terms of a contract create the rights and obligations of the parties. To represent them faithfully, financial statements report their **substance**. Sometimes the substance is clear from the legal form; other times the terms, or a **group or series of contracts**, need analysis.

- **All terms count**, explicit or implicit, unless they **have no substance**. Implicit terms could be obligations imposed by statute, for example **statutory warranty obligations** on contracts to sell goods.
- **Terms with no substance are disregarded.** A term has no substance if it has **no discernible effect on the economics** of the contract. Examples: terms that **bind neither party**, or rights (including options) the holder will **not have the practical ability to exercise** in any circumstances.
- A **group or series of contracts** may be designed to achieve an overall commercial effect. Then it may be necessary to treat their rights and obligations as a **single unit of account**. For example, if one contract **cancels out** all rights and obligations of another contract made at the same time with the same counterparty, the combined effect is that **no rights or obligations** exist.
- Conversely, if a single contract creates two or more sets of rights and obligations that could have been created by separate contracts, the entity may need to **account for each set as if it came from a separate contract**.
chunks.exam_line: Statements report the substance of contract terms. Terms with no substance are disregarded; contracts that cancel each other out may be combined into one unit.

questions.stem: What is a unit of account and what is it chosen to achieve?
questions.model_answer_md:
The **unit of account** is the right or group of rights, the obligation or group of obligations, or the group of rights and obligations, **to which recognition criteria and measurement concepts are applied**.

It is chosen to give **useful information**: it must be **relevant** (a group may be better if the items cannot be sold separately, do not expire in different patterns, have similar characteristics and risks, or are used together) and must **faithfully represent the substance** of the transaction. **Cost** also constrains the choice, because costs generally rise as the unit gets smaller.

questions.stem: Explain how an executory contract is treated and what happens when one party performs.
questions.model_answer_md:
An **executory contract** is equally unperformed. It creates a **combined right and obligation to exchange economic resources**, interdependent and inseparable, so together they are **one asset or liability**: an **asset** if the terms are currently favourable, a **liability** if unfavourable. Whether it appears depends on the recognition criteria and measurement basis, including any onerous contract test.

When a party **performs**, the contract is no longer executory. If the **entity performs first**, its position becomes a **right to receive** a resource, an **asset**. If the **other party performs first**, it becomes an **obligation to transfer** a resource, a **liability**.

questions.stem: Explain what 'substance' means for contract terms and give examples of terms that are disregarded.
questions.model_answer_md:
To represent rights and obligations faithfully, statements report their **substance**. All terms, **explicit or implicit**, are considered unless they **have no substance**. Implicit terms could include statutory obligations such as warranty obligations on contracts to sell goods.

A term has **no substance** if it has no discernible effect on the economics of the contract, and is disregarded. Examples: terms that **bind neither party**, or rights (including options) the holder **cannot practically exercise in any circumstances**.

A group or series of contracts may be treated as a single unit if designed for an overall commercial effect; for instance two contracts at the same time with the same counterparty that cancel each other create no rights or obligations.

questions.stem: Discuss the unit of account concept: what it is, how it is chosen and the possible units.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Meaning.** The unit of account is the right or group of rights, the obligation or group of obligations, or the group of rights and obligations, to which recognition criteria and measurement concepts are applied. It can differ for recognition and measurement (contracts recognised individually but measured as a portfolio), and presentation and disclosure may aggregate or separate items. If part of an item is transferred, the unit may change.

**Choice.** The unit is chosen to give **useful information**:

- **Relevance:** a group may be better where its rights and obligations cannot be or are unlikely to be sold separately, do not expire in different patterns, have similar characteristics and risks, or are used together to produce cash flows measured by interdependent estimates.
- **Faithful representation of substance:** it may be necessary to treat rights from different sources as one unit or to separate rights from a single source.
- **Cost:** costs generally rise as the unit gets smaller, so same-source rights are separated only if more useful and benefits outweigh costs.

**Rights and obligations from one source.** If interdependent and inseparable they are a single asset or liability (as with executory contracts); if separable they may be grouped separately or together. This differs from offsetting.

**Possible units:** an individual right or obligation; all rights or obligations from a contract; a subgroup; a portfolio of similar items; a portfolio of dissimilar items; or a risk exposure within a portfolio.

rubric.point: Definition and difference between recognition and measurement units
Interdependent rights and obligations; not offsetting

questions.stem: Explain executory contracts and the substance of contractual rights and obligations, with the role of terms that have no substance.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Executory contracts.** A contract equally unperformed. It creates a combined, inseparable right and obligation to exchange resources, forming one asset (if terms are favourable) or one liability (if unfavourable). Whether it is in the statements depends on recognition and measurement. If the entity performs first, the combination becomes a right to receive (an asset); if the other party performs first, an obligation to transfer (a liability). An example elsewhere is a salary contract before the services are received.

**Substance.** The statements report the substance of the rights and obligations created by contract terms. Sometimes it is clear from the legal form; sometimes terms or a series of contracts need analysis. All terms, explicit or implicit (such as statutory warranty obligations), count unless they have no substance. Terms with **no discernible effect on the economics**, such as terms that bind neither party or options that cannot practically be exercised, are **disregarded**.

**Groups of contracts.** A group or series designed to achieve an overall commercial effect may need to be a single unit of account; contracts that cancel each other create no rights or obligations. A single contract that creates sets of rights that could arise from separate contracts may be accounted for as separate sets.
